data.title: Amnesic Probing: Behavioral Explanation with Amnesic Counterfactuals
data.abstract: A growing body of work makes use of probing to investigate the working of neural models, often considered black boxes. Recently, an ongoing debate emerged surrounding the limitations of the probing paradigm. In this work, we point out the inability to infer behavioral conclusions from probing results and offer an alternative method that focuses on how the information is being used, rather than on what information is encoded. Our method, Amnesic Probing, follows the intuition that the utility of a property for a given task can be assessed by measuring the influence of a causal intervention that removes it from the representation. Equipped with this new analysis tool, we can ask questions that were not possible before, e.g. is part-of-speech information important for word prediction? We perform a series of analyses on BERT to answer these types of questions. Our findings demonstrate that conventional probing performance is not correlated to task importance, and we call for increased scrutiny of claims that draw behavioral or causal conclusions from probing results.
data.tldr: Amnesic Probing measures task importance by intervening on representations to remove a property, rather than testing whether it is encoded. On BERT, probe accuracy does not correlate with behavioral influence, challenging causal conclusions drawn from conventional probing.

preview.name: Probing
preview.description: In AI, "probing" refers to using techniques to understand and analyze the internal workings of a model. Probing classifiers involves training small, simple models (probes) on a target model's learned representations to see what information (like syntax or semantics) is encoded within them. An example of this could be training a logistic regression or linear classifier on top of a model's pre-train
